newsitem.title: USA: US legislator likely to resubmit encryption bill.
newsitem.headline: US legislator likely to resubmit encryption bill.

text.p: One of the primary Congressional critics of U.S. encryption export limits said Wednesday he would likely reintroduce a bill next month to ease the rules substantially.
Rep. Bob Goodlatte also criticized moves by the Clinton administration to modestly ease the Cold war era export rules.

"The administration continues to take two steps back for every step they take forward," the Virginia Republican said in a statement. "The rules they are proposing violate the privacy of U.S. citizens, cost American jobs and kill the ability of U.S. software companies to compete effectively abroad."
Encryption programs use mathematical formulas to scramble information, such as an electronic mail message, and render it unreadable without a password or software key.

Under an executive order signed by President Bill Clinton Nov. 15, U.S. companies would be allowed to export products containing strong encryption but only if the government was able to unscramble coded messages by recovering the keys.

A spokeswoman for the Commerce Department, which is drafting rules to implement the new Clinton policy, said the administration had no immediate comment on Goodlatte's statement but might issue a response later on Wednesday.
Sen. Conrad Burns, a Republican from Montana, will resubmit his bill "probably no earlier than the beginning of February," spokesman Matt Raymond said.
The bill could be identical to the previous version or contain modifications to address concerns raised by some Senators earlier this year, Raymond said.
Commerce Department has said it expects to issue rules implementing the new Clinton export policy by January 1, 1997.
